reasoning.Student A:
Given that most applicants prefer y > x > w > z, and I strongly prefer w, I need to consider how to maximize my chances of getting into w. If I rank w first, as I naturally would, the question becomes how to handle the other schools.

If I rank z second, and y third, and x last, I'm signaling that I'm willing to go to z if w doesn't work out. However, since most others prefer y, y will likely be very competitive. If I rank y second, I might get "stuck" proposing to y repeatedly while w remains open to someone who prefers it less.

Since I have a high priority at y (rank 1), and most others prefer it, I might be able to get y if w doesn't work out. However, w is my strongest preference. I have a good priority at w (1) and x (2). I also have a good priority at y (1). Z is my least preferred, and I have a lower priority there (2).

Considering the deferred acceptance algorithm, and the other students' preferences, I believe the best strategy is to stick with my true preferences. If I try to game the system by ranking a less-preferred school higher, hoping to get a fallback, I might end up losing out on w altogether. I'll propose to w first, and if rejected, move down my list. The fact that most people prefer y means that w might be less competitive than it would otherwise be.
